title: Gametic and non-gametic parental resources and the definition of sexual selection: a comment on Janicke
content: In The Origin, Darwin conceptualized sexual selection as the “struggle between the males for possession of the females,” later refining this definition to “the advantage which certain individuals have over other individuals of the same sex and species, in exclusive relation to reproduction” in The Descent. Darwin’s apparent broadening of his definition has generated debate over whether competition for access to resources required for reproduction should be considered sexual selection or natural selection, in particular when females compete for resources (Clutton-Brock 2009). To clarify what we mean by sexual selection, Shuker and Kvarnemo (2021) suggested a new definition as “any selection that arises from fitness differences associated with nonrandom success in the competition for access to gametes for fertilization.” This gamete-centered definition has considerable merit, because it includes what we now understand about selection that continues after mate acquisition, via post-copulatory mechanisms of gamete competition and choice (Simmons and Parker 2021). It also has the advantage of being agnostic with respect to sex, and inclusive of all sexually reproducing organisms from broadcast spawners to internal fertilizers. However, a gamete-centered definition raises its own problems, because rarely are individuals limited in their ability to reproduce by gametes alone.
